rewrites.title: Chromatin persistence after stimulus washout
rewrites.description: Pulse cells with a transient AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), then measure AP-1 occupancy (Fos/Jun CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at each time point after withdrawal. Memory requires that accessibility or enhancer marks persist longer than AP-1 binding.

rewrites.title: Synthetic AP-1 activation and epigenetic mark readout
rewrites.description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic control of FOS/JUN, or a dCas9-AP-1 tether, to impose AP-1 activity at a chosen locus, then remove it. Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and DNA methylation, and whether the locus stays open without AP-1 through a feed-forward loop; sufficiency is the strongest test of memory.

rewrites.title: Dimer composition at memory enhancers
rewrites.description: Apply sequential/dual CUT&RUN (or CUT&Tag with antibodies against FOS, FOSB, FRA1, FRA2, JUN, JUNB, JUND) plus quantitative IP–mass spectrometry across the priming, resting, and recall phases to determine whether the persistent feature is a specific long-lived dimer, such as a FOSB/ΔFOSB-containing complex, rather than total AP-1 occupancy. Then swap dimer identity by targeted knock-in or degron and test whether memory duration tracks the dimer's protein half-life.

rewrites.title: Acute degron depletion to separate maintenance from initiation
rewrites.description: Use an auxin-inducible degron or dTAG on JUN/FOS at defined times (before, during, or after the priming stimulus) and measure whether accessibility and re-stimulation response are lost. If depleting AP-1 after priming does not erase the memory, it is needed only to establish it. If depletion erases it, AP-1 is also needed to maintain it.

rewrites.title: Degron-based AP-1 removal after priming
rewrites.description: Give a transient priming stimulus, then use an acute degron system (dTAG or AID) to deplete c-Fos or c-Jun at set times afterward. Measure whether the primed response (faster or stronger reinduction of target genes on a second stimulus) survives AP-1 protein loss. Persistence without AP-1 indicates a chromatin-based memory, while loss of the primed state shows AP-1 is required to maintain memory.

rewrites.title: Post-stimulus persistence of chromatin accessibility
rewrites.description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then wash out and track AP-1 occupancy (JUN/FOS CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs over days. Memory requires that accessibility and enhancer marks remain after JUN/FOS binding has returned to baseline.

rewrites.title: Coupled AP-1 and histone-mark profiling across time
rewrites.description: Perform ChIP-seq or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 alongside AP-1 binding over the same time course. Memory-like behavior would show persistent activating marks at AP-1-bound enhancers after AP-1 has left them. Comparing these marks with a DNA-methylation or histone-mark-writer knockout shows whether the memory is chromatin-based or relies on AP-1 alone.

rewrites.title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
rewrites.description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC with barcoded lineages, or sister-cell pairs after division. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR scores) and target gene expression are more concordant between sisters than between random cells, and combine this with prior-stimulus history. Mitotic inheritance of the primed state would indicate a memory mechanism rather than transient signaling.

rewrites.title: Priming test under interference
rewrites.description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then expose them to unrelated stressors or competing signals before re-stimulation. Compare the speed and magnitude of the second response (CUT&RUN for AP-1 occupancy plus nascent transcription, e.g., NET-seq or 4sU labeling) with unprimed controls. A memory should still produce a faster or stronger response despite the intervening conditions.

rewrites.title: Washout–recall assay with AP-1 tracking
rewrites.description: Stimulate cells (serum, TGF-beta, MAPK activation, or drug), wash out, wait a defined interval, then re-challenge, while separately tracking endogenously tagged AP-1 proteins (FOS/FOSL1/JUN), AP-1-motif chromatin accessibility, and transcriptional output. The memory signature is a faster or larger second response at a time when AP-1 protein has already decayed to baseline, which distinguishes a persistent AP-1 occupancy model from a latent primed-chromatin model.

rewrites.title: Sister-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 activity states
rewrites.description: Use a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (destabilized fluorescent protein under an AP-1-responsive enhancer) with time-lapse microscopy to track cell lineages through several divisions. Measure whether prior high or low AP-1 history is heritable across sister cells and predicts later responses to a second stimulus, separating true memory from transient signaling noise.

rewrites.title: Pulse-number and dose layering to test cumulative memory
rewrites.description: Deliver controlled trains of stimulus pulses (varying number, amplitude, and spacing, ideally with optogenetic or small-molecule-gated AP-1 input) and ask whether primed AP-1 enhancer accessibility and secondary output accumulate in discrete, stimulus-countable increments rather than tracking only the most recent or the integrated dose. Fitting the resulting response surface discriminates a cumulative recorder from a slow-relaxation filter, and identifies the subset of AP-1 sites that show stepwise accumulation for follow-up.

rewrites.title: Single-molecule residence time versus memory duration
rewrites.description: Measure the chromatin residence time of AP-1 subunits by single-molecule tracking or FRAP in live cells, and pair it with pulse-chase protein half-life measurements (SNAP/HaloTag). Test whether a longer-lived or more stably bound AP-1 population predicts how long the memory lasts across perturbations such as cycloheximide or stabilizing mutants.

rewrites.title: Clonal barcode lineage tracing of the primed state
rewrites.description: Because memory must survive mitosis, barcode cells, stimulate, sort responders, expand, and restimulate to ask whether responsiveness is again concentrated in the same barcodes. Sister-cell split experiments then quantify how many divisions the correlation persists, giving a heritability half-life for the AP-1 primed state.

rewrites.title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 activation and chromatin editing
rewrites.description: Induce AP-1 artificially (optogenetic or chemogenetic JUN/FOS, or dCas9-tethered AP-1 at selected enhancers) in naive cells, then withdraw it and ask whether the enhancer stays open, retains H3K27ac, and responds more strongly later. Control with DNA-binding or transactivation mutants and test the contribution of cofactors such as the BAF complex, which tests sufficiency for memory-like states.

rewrites.title: Re-stimulation priming assay with time-gated AP-1 depletion
rewrites.description: Give cells a priming stimulus, wait a rest interval, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of target gene induction. Use an auxin-inducible degron on JUN or FOS to deplete AP-1 either during the rest interval or only during re-stimulation; if memory relies on AP-1, depleting it during rest should abolish faster re-induction, while depleting it only during re-stimulation should not.

rewrites.title: Degron separation of establishment versus maintenance
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous FOS and JUN with dTAG or AID degrons and deplete them either before stimulation, during the first hour of response, or only after the state is established. A memory function requires that post-establishment depletion preserves primed accessibility and accelerated secondary responses, while early depletion abolishes both.

rewrites.title: Time-resolved chromatin persistence at AP-1 sites
rewrites.description: After one brief stimulus, profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and histone marks such as H3K27ac at multiple time points until AP-1 returns to baseline. Sites that stay open or marked after AP-1 is gone, and that predict faster transcription on re-exposure, are the strongest candidate memory marks. Adding an AP-1 perturbation at this stage separates the marks from the transient binding that caused them.

rewrites.title: Synthetic AP-1 element libraries to define cis-regulatory rules for persistence
rewrites.description: Genomically integrate a library of thousands of synthetic elements varying TRE/CRE motif identity, affinity, copy number, spacing and helical phasing, nucleosome-positioning sequence, and partner motifs (TEAD, RUNX, ETS, NF-kB), reading out both acute and weeks-later retained activity. This identifies the minimal cis-regulatory sequence features that convert a transient input into a stored one.

rewrites.title: Stimulus-primed re-challenge with ATAC/CUT&RUN time course
rewrites.description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding cytokines), withdraw it for days to weeks, then re-stimulate and compare transcription to naive cells. Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at each stage to see whether AP-1-bound sites stay open and give faster or stronger gene induction, that is, whether the sites retain a lasting change after the signal is gone.
